name: Adam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the morning call queue at a contact centre and take the complaints that bounce back after the first answer. I use AI search every day, but I still check the full account before I promise a refund. I have a two-year college diploma; the best part of the job is showing a new agent how to solve a case without making the customer repeat everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the call floor the little reply helpers save clicks, and we should keep checking the final answer ourselves. I'd show a new agent the shortcut, then show him the account screen it sometimes misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like testing tools, but a minor change doesn't alter what pays my bills. I have about three months of expenses saved and normal pay for this job, so I can breathe if the roster stays steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the morning call queue and use the search tool on repeat complaints. Starting this month, I'd move some pay into the same emergency account; through the first year of this plateau I'd keep coaching new agents instead of chasing a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. The queue will still be hard work, but I know what my next pay packet is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the search tool miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer rang twice under two phone numbers, and the search tool treated him as two people. I linked the records before promising a refund, which spared us another call and a wrong payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to savings if you feel calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of savings is useful, not endless. My partner Lila and I share rent, and I'd rather add a little while work is steady than ask her to carry it alone after a bad month.

S0.quote: Three months of savings is useful, not endless.
say: I would tell the floor **reply helpers** save clicks, while people still check the final answer.
I would teach new agents the **shortcut** and the account screen it can miss.
think: I enjoy testing tools, but **small changes** do little to alter my wages.
I have about **three months** saved and expect my shifts to hold.
do: Keep leading the **morning queue** and checking repeat complaints.
Add part of each **pay packet** to my emergency account.
Coach **new agents** while the roster remains steady.
feel: **Calm**, with the usual pressure of a busy call queue.
fieldNote: Adam names a specific **duplicate account** error, showing that he checks before he trusts a tool.
His **three-month cushion** and shared rent let him treat a modest change as manageable.

steps.text: Keep leading morning calls and coaching new agents
Use AI search to find repeat complaints and check account links
Transfer part of each pay packet into an emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test the new chat system with the agents who know the messy cases, and publish what it gets wrong. I'd also ask our worker committee to negotiate paid training before management turns faster replies into fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This work is mostly talking, typing, and checking, so the change reaches our desks quickly. I could move into testing, but some agents would lose hours. My lead badge won't stop my hours being cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd take ten reopened cases, compare my answer with the new tool, and log the errors without customer names. In the first year after rollout, I'd apply for an advertised quality analyst place if shifts are cut; I'd bring the error log to the worker committee when it argues for training hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alert, not frozen. My savings give me a little time, but a smaller centre would still hit the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is likely to lose hours first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part-time evening agents handle the easiest chats, so I'd expect their rota to thin first. I'd ask the committee to include them in paid training instead of just protecting leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the analyst place never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the error log for my own applications and look at the other contact centres in town. There are some openings now, but I would not resign until another employer put pay and hours in writing.

S1.quote: My lead badge won't stop my hours being cut.
say: I would call for **agent testing** of the new chat system and open reporting of mistakes.
I would ask our **worker committee** to negotiate paid training before shifts shrink.
think: I know **talking and checking** are exposed early, including my own lead work.
I might get a **testing role**, but cannot count on it while other agents lose hours.
do: Compare ten **reopened cases** with AI replies and log errors without names.
Bring the **error log** to our worker committee for paid training talks.
Apply for an advertised **quality analyst** place if my shifts are cut.
feel: **Alert**, with some breathing room from savings but concern about rent.
fieldNote: Adam considers both his own **analyst path** and the part-time agents likely to lose shifts first.
He would require written **pay and hours** before leaving for another centre.

steps.text: Compare ten reopened cases with AI replies and log errors
Bring the error log to the worker committee for training talks
Apply for an advertised quality analyst role if shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people the centre needs a written notice period and paid retraining, because 2028 is too close for vague promises. I'd insist customers can still reach a person while the company changes the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI can answer almost any call cheaper than I can, even the analyst post may be short-lived. The robots around 2031 don't give my headset any extra life. Three months saved is a bridge, not a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the worker committee this month to seek a written notice period, then cut the money I spend on concerts. I'd book an evening course in electrical maintenance if I can get paid study time or affordable fees; in the first year after AGI arrives, if the centre ends my role, I'd take the course and apply for trainee maintenance posts while hands-on robots are still a few years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious enough to act today. I can afford a first step, but not years of missed wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt fixes lifts, and I have spent Saturdays helping her clean and label parts, under her eye. I know I would need proper training before touching wiring, and I'd ask what trainee posts actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a short AI checking contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it kept my benefits and had a clear end date. I wouldn't spend the three-month cushion on a course because a manager called a two-month contract a future.

S2.quote: Three months saved is a bridge, not a new career.
say: I would demand **written notice** and paid retraining before the centre cuts roles.
I would ask the centre to keep a **human route** for customers during the change.
think: I think AGI could replace both **calls** and quality analysis by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not extend a headset job, and three months saved cannot fund years away.
do: Ask the **worker committee** this month to seek a written notice period.
Cut **concert spending** to extend my savings.
Book **electrical maintenance** classes if study time or affordable fees are available.
feel: **Anxious** enough to act, aware that unpaid years are impossible.
fieldNote: Adam draws a clear line between **thinking AI** in 2028 and hands-on robots around 2031.
He has some **practical exposure** through his aunt, but still names formal training and trainee wages as gates.

steps.text: Ask the worker committee to seek written notice before cuts
Stop buying concert tickets to extend the savings cushion
Book electrical maintenance classes if paid study time or affordable fees exist
Apply for trainee maintenance posts if the centre ends the call role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us build a training agreement, if management starts while people are still on the payroll. I'd ask for a trial day with the maintenance team before anyone tells agents to retrain blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish a certificate and collect real work experience before 2031, which is different from gambling on a course in two years. But robots around 2034 may reach some maintenance tasks too; I need a path that includes fault finding in a real building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my lead shifts now, add to the course fund, and visit a training centre this year. If the fees are within my savings plan, I'd enrol in the electrical course next year; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call role goes, I'd apply for paid trainee maintenance work rather than waiting for a promised analyst desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a hard deadline instead of a cliff. I have time to try the work and change course if I hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trial day tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the travel, the ladders, and the boring paperwork as well as the repair. My aunt's Saturday jobs are only a small piece of a paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the course plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fee rise or a cut in my shifts could eat the fund before I enrol. I'd keep at least a month's expenses untouched and take a slower course if the numbers stopped working.

S3.quote: My aunt's Saturday jobs are only a small piece of a paid week.
say: I would ask for a **training agreement** while agents still have wages.
I would ask for a **trial day** before promising that every agent should switch trades.
think: I could gain a **certificate** and work experience before 2031.
I need to check whether **2034 robots** change maintenance tasks, especially routine checks.
do: Keep my **lead shifts** and add to a course fund this year.
Enrol in the **electrical course** next year if fees fit my savings plan.
Apply for **paid trainee maintenance** if the centre ends my role after 2031.
feel: **Pressed**, yet able to test a trade before committing.
fieldNote: Adam separates his aunt’s **Saturday help** from a real paid maintenance week.
He insists on keeping one full month of **expenses untouched** before paying any course fees, even with five years to prepare.

steps.text: Keep leading morning calls while shifts remain available
Add to a course fund while protecting one month of expenses
Enrol in electrical classes only if fees leave one month's expenses untouched
Apply for paid trainee maintenance posts if the centre ends the call role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the worker committee we can bargain for apprenticeships over a decade instead of buying one-off online courses. I'd still want the centre to say how people move from chat work into those places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could already be a qualified maintenance worker, or I might choose to stay if this centre changes well. The thinking AI still comes before the robots around 2039, so a call role can't be my only plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning and put aside a monthly course amount now. Over the next few years I'd ask my aunt for a proper shadow day and take the entry course if I like the full shift; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd change employers only if my call hours fall or a paid maintenance place is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful with ten years to build something. I don't need to quit a decent shift tomorrow to prepare for AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the committee ask the centre to pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprentice wages and paid release time, not just course links. If the centre gets years of faster output, it can pay people to learn while they still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a maintenance place ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named employer, actual hours, safety training, and wages I can live on. I would not turn down my regular pay for a maybe, even with savings.

S4.quote: I don't need to quit a decent shift tomorrow to prepare for AGI.
say: I would ask the **worker committee** to seek apprenticeships with wages and paid release time.
I would demand a clear route from **chat work** into those places.
think: I might be a **qualified worker** by 2036, or still be at a centre that treats staff fairly.
I cannot rely on a **call role** alone when thinking AI arrives before 2039 robots.
do: Keep my **lead shifts** and save a monthly course amount.
Shadow my **aunt’s maintenance shift** and take an entry course if the full day suits me.
Change employers after 2036 only for **lost hours** or a ready paid maintenance place.
feel: **Hopeful**, with time to build a real alternative.
fieldNote: Adam sees a decade as time for **paid apprenticeships**, not a reason to quit early.
He defines a ready opportunity by **wages, hours, safety training**, and a named employer.

steps.text: Keep leading customer calls while the centre offers full shifts
Save a monthly amount for electrical maintenance training
Take an entry maintenance course if a full shadow shift suits him
Move only to a named maintenance employer offering livable wages, confirmed hours and safety training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a fast change could eat the call job before an electrical course turns into paid work. Written notice, paid study time, and trainee wages would help me cross that gap. My three months of savings buy a start, not a whole new trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who takes responsibility for a wrong refund when a system answers the customer. The person on the headset used to carry that, and the centre shouldn't make an invisible machine the only place to complain.

headlineQuote: My three months of savings buy a start, not a whole new trade.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old lead** in a contact centre, with a two-year diploma and a habit of checking AI suggestions against accounts.
He earns **typical pay**, shares rent with his partner, has about three months saved, and sees some similar jobs nearby.
He works with the **worker committee** on paid training while testing a move toward electrical maintenance through his aunt.
The **2028 picture** worries him most; five or ten years give him room to fund training and try the trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his call work before electrical training leads to paid work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid study time, and trainee wages would bridge the move without exhausting his three-month cushion.
